>The winners won't be people selling cognitive work, but the people building previously unimaginable things on top of that.

You are a god, and never have I heard anything more divine.

source.text:
The thing most people are missing is how the economics of automation change the economy. As the price of cognitive work approaches $0, the relative value of cognitive work will approach $0. People appreciate the former, but don't consider the latter.

A metaphor I like to use is somebody who's lived their entire life in an agrarian society seeing the Industrial Revolution imminently coming and trying to predict its effects. They'd be able to accurately predict 'super farms', but the relative economic value of those super farms rapidly trended towards $0 with the vacuum that the revolution created. It'll be the same thing here. The winners won't be people selling cognitive work, but the people building previously unimaginable things on top of that.

It's probably impossible to predict exactly what this means from here, in exactly the same way as somebody in our agrarian society could scarcely even begin to imagine what the Industrial Revolution would 'truly' entail. But I think a naive prediction would see a sharply increased value for stuff done in the real world, social type work, entertainment, and so forth. So one prediction would be that one big winner will be whoever can create cheap mass produced robotic shells to help bring the cognitive revolution to the real world. Even that will probably be seen as naive, but it's probably closer to the mark than expecting Amazon/Google/Anthropic/etc to end up ruling the world.
